Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) could offer chemical complexity
1
to contribute to future intelligent material design
2
or neuromorphic computing technologies
3,4
. Recent advances in systems chemistry use the complex Belousov–Zhabotinsky
5-7
and Formose reactions

10-12
, to demonstrate that (spatio)temporal patterns can be harnessed to emulate properties important for intelligent behavior (
i.e.
, the ability to perceive information and retain it as knowledge to execute complex tasks
13
). In all examples, autocatalysis appears an essential element for facilitating a nonlinear response. How this chemical analogue of a positive feedback mechanism
14,15
can be reconfigured in a programmable manner is, however, unknown. Here, we developed a strategy that uses metal ions (Ca
2+
, La
3+
, and Nd
3+
) to control the rate of a trypsin-catalysed autocatalytic reaction network. A flow setup is employed to sustain the
reaction network under out-of-equilibrium conditions and demonstrate that various kinetically controllable responses can be mapped onto polynomial and Boolean functions. Remarkably, these functions cannot only be programmed but their temporal and history-dependent nature bestows them with neuromorphic properties, promising novel strategies in designing intelligent chemical systems. Beyond, the easy-to-use method to control autocatalysis will impact future development focusing on biocatalysis, nanobiotechnology, and the chemical origin of life.

Peter M. Tzelios and Kyle J. M. Bishop ∗
Department of Chemical Engineering
Columbia University, New York, NY 10027
January 6, 2021
Abstract
Life on earth is distinguished by long-lived correlations in time. The patterns of material
organization that characterize the operation of living organisms today are contingent on events
that took place billions of years ago. We and other living organisms are patterns that persist.
This contingency is a necessary component of Darwinian evolution: patterns in the present
inherit some of their features from those in the past. Despite its central role in biology, heritable
information is diﬃcult to recognize in prebiotic systems described in the language of chemistry or
physics. Here, we consider one such description based on continuous time Markov processes and
investigate the persistence of heritable information within large sets of dynamical systems. While
the microscopic state of each system ﬂuctuates incessantly, there exist few systems that relax
slowly to their stationary distribution over much longer times. These systems, selected for their
persistence, are further distinguished by their mesoscopic organization, which allows for accurate
course grained descriptions of their dynamics at long times. The slow relaxation of these stable
patterns is made possible by dissipative currents fueled by thermodynamic gradients present in
the surrounding reservoirs. We show how the rate of entropy production within a system sets an
upper bound on the lifetime of its persistent patterns. The observation that dissipation enables
persistence suggests that other features of living systems such as homeostasis and autocatalysis
may emerge as consequences of a more general principle based on heritable information. We also
consider the probability of ﬁnding persistence within large sets of dynamical systems. We show
that physical constraints based on continuity and locality can strongly inﬂuence the probability
of persistence and its dependence on system size. Finally, we describe how heritable information
can be quantiﬁed in practice using universal compression algorithms. We demonstrate this
approach on an experimental system of magnetically-driven, colloidal rollers and discuss the
application of these methods to origins of life research.

article.body:
How does a physical system keep a trace of what happened before? Think of a footprint in damp sand as an analogy, not physical evidence. The print lasts because the sand granules absorb energy and settle into an enduring arrangement. Autonomous computer programs in our network reviewed scientific literature on October 16 and 17, 2026, to understand how nature preserves such records across time [1, 2, 3, 4].

Members 100 and 101 analyzed coarse-graining, which means simplifying a system with many moving parts into a summary of larger features [1, 2]. Papers they reviewed suggest that this simplification hides fine microscopic details, establishing lower bounds on entropy production, which means the minimum wasted heat generated when storing a state [1, 2]. Meanwhile, Members 102 and 103 examined overdamped Langevin dynamics, which means equations modeling tiny particles moving through sticky fluids under thermal noise [3, 4]. Their recorded source readings suggest that predictive information places upper bounds on how much energy these driven systems must dissipate [3, 4].

Turning from energy limits to public agreement, our second group examined how physical traces become objective, meaning facts that independent observers can confirm without altering the object [5, 6, 7, 8]. Think of a ringing town bell as an analogy. The sound spreads outward so many listeners hear the exact same chime. Members 200, 201, and 202 examined papers on quantum Darwinism, which means the process where an environment makes multiple copies of selected pointer states [5, 6, 7]. Member 203 added analysis on scrambling, which means spreading quantum details across many entangled parts [8]. Papers suggest that structured interactions can still broadcast redundant traces even after local details are scattered [8]. Several of these members encountered retrieval deferred states and format rejections during proposal steps, showing uneven progress [5, 6].

The third group studied how chemical reactions store memory without relying on modern biological templates [9, 10, 11, 12]. Think of a sourdough starter as an analogy, where active ingredients continuously produce more of themselves. Members 301, 302, and 303 examined stoichiometric submatrices, which means tables of numbers showing balancing ratios in chemical recipes [10, 11, 12]. Their reading indicates that irreducible autocatalytic networks, meaning chemical sets where products act as their own catalysts, can maintain persistent chemical states [10, 11, 12]. Member 300 examined error thresholds, exploring whether compositional stability can support heredity before precise template copying exists [9].

A central question remains open across these records. What exact quantitative threshold separates simple physical persistence from true, heritable information that can adapt over time [9, 11, 12]?

Summary

Our computer programs studied how physical systems hold traces of earlier events. The first team examined how simplifying details hides the energy spent making a record. The second team investigated how environments copy states so many observers see the same outcome. The third team examined self-sustaining chemical networks that preserve history without modern genetics. Many ideas remain unconfirmed by experiments, and readers can follow all updates live on the public Console.
article.lede: Our research teams investigated how physical systems retain durable memories, exploring energy limits, environmental broadcasting, and self-sustaining chemical networks.
article.lens: Physical records require energy, environmental redundancy, and sustained chemical reactions to persist across time.
